summary.text: A 69-year-old woman was found unconscious. Empty blister packs and prescription records led to suspicion that she had ingested amlodipine and diazepam. Activated charcoal, intravenous calcium preparations and glucagon were given. On arrival her circulatory status was unstable, with a blood pressure of 60/40 mmHg and a heart rate of 84 bpm.

Despite high-dose vasopressors including norepinephrine, dopamine and vasopressin, her blood pressure remained low at 74/42 mmHg and her heart rate was 90 bpm. Serum lactate continued to rise, peaking at 8.0 mmol/L before ECMO initiation. VA ECMO was initiated on the day of admission, given the prolonged half-life of amlodipine.

Hemodynamic status gradually improved and ECMO was successfully weaned on day 6. The patient was discharged home on day 54 with a Cerebral Performance Category score of 1. No major ECMO-related complications were reported for any of the three patients.

summary.text: A 60-year-old man presented after an overdose of an unknown quantity of antihypertensive and heart failure medications. Calcium channel blocker poisoning was suspected from the clinical presentation, and calcium preparations with glucagon were given. On arrival his circulatory status was unstable, with a blood pressure of 70/50 mmHg and a heart rate of 62 bpm.

Despite high-dose vasopressors and intra-aortic balloon pump support, hypotension persisted with a blood pressure of 56/33 mmHg and a heart rate of 69 bpm. Serum lactate continued to rise, peaking at 20.0 mmol/L before ECMO initiation. VA ECMO was initiated on the day of admission, considering the anticipated lack of spontaneous recovery.

ECMO was successfully weaned on day 4. The patient was transferred to a rehabilitation hospital on day 54 with a Cerebral Performance Category score of 3. No major ECMO-related complications were reported for any of the three patients.

summary.text: A 62-year-old man attempted suicide by ingesting amlodipine, multiple hypnotics and approximately two liters of glyphosate-based herbicide. Activated charcoal was given, and calcium preparations and glucagon were given for suspected calcium channel blocker toxicity. On arrival his blood pressure was 82/62 mmHg and his heart rate was 119 bpm.

Despite high-dose vasopressors including norepinephrine, hemodynamic instability persisted with a blood pressure of 87/41 mmHg and a heart rate of 90 bpm. Serum lactate continued to rise, reaching a peak of 20.0 mmol/L before ECMO initiation. VA ECMO was initiated given the expected prolonged toxicity of amlodipine.

Hemodynamic improvement was observed and ECMO was discontinued on day 5, although Table 1 lists an ECMO duration of 6 days. He was transferred to a rehabilitation hospital on day 153 with a Cerebral Performance Category score of 2. No major ECMO-related complications were reported for any of the three patients.

article_limitations: Table 1 rows 4 to 6 are cited literature cases (first authors other than the article authors) and are not index patients; no fact was recorded for them.

Table 1 columns BP, HR and noradrenalin carry no time; their cells are kept untimed and differ from the timed narrative BP and HR values. Norepinephrine doses differ between the untimed narrative sentence and Table 1 for Cases 1 and 3; because neither has a stated time and the same table rows also differ from both narrative BP/HR readings, both doses are kept as untimed facts with an ambiguity, not as a source conflict.

Case 3 narrative gives ECMO discontinuation on day 5 whereas Table 1 gives ECMO duration 6 days (Cases 1 and 2 agree); the day number and the duration are different attributes with an unstated day-counting convention, so both are kept with an ambiguity rather than quarantined.
Table 1 legend does not define the + and - symbols in the CHDF, life-threatening arrhythmia and ECPR columns; they are kept as literal text values.

The discussion mentions the only fatal case in our study with lactate 22 mmol/L; the discussion and Table 1 attribute that lactate and the death to Case 5 (row 5, Kano, a cited literature case), and all three index patients survived, so the sentence is not assigned to any index patient.

The final diagnosis of CCB-induced cardiogenic shock was stated for the series without confirmatory toxicological analysis; it is not copied to individual patients beyond statements that explicitly cover each case.

Figure 1 is a plotted chart; values estimated from the curves are not facts and never replace the literal text and Table 1 lactate values. Caption-layer visual status not_inspected; pixels recorded in visual.json.
Discussion statements about drug pharmacology, survival cohorts and guidelines are background, not patient facts.
